title: Arithmetic Progressions — Complete Learning Module
outcomes: Identify arithmetic progressions (AP) from given sequences
Find the nth term of an AP using aₙ = a + (n-1)d
Calculate the sum of n terms of an AP using Sₙ = n/2[2a + (n-1)d]
Insert arithmetic means between given numbers
Apply AP concepts to real-life Indian context problems
Solve RD Sharma and RS Aggarwal extension problems for competitive exam readiness

concepts.name: Arithmetic Progression — The Pattern of Equal Steps
concepts.real_life_application: Ravi saves ₹100 in the first week, ₹150 in the second, ₹200 in the third — each week ₹50 more. His savings are in AP: 100, 150, 200, 250, ... The common difference is ₹50. This is how systematic savings, loan repayments, and even ticket prices for metro rides (₹10 for 1st station, ₹15 for 2nd, ₹20 for 3rd) follow AP.
concepts.purpose: An AP is a sequence where each term increases (or decreases) by a constant value called the 'common difference.' It's the simplest and most natural pattern — from the rows in a theatre (each row has 2 more seats) to the daily savings in a piggy bank.
day_to_day_usage: Metro fare: ₹10 for 1 km, ₹15 for 2 km, ₹20 for 3 km (d = ₹5)
Monthly savings: ₹500 in January, ₹550 in February, ₹600 in March (d = ₹50)
Seats in an auditorium: 20 in row 1, 24 in row 2, 28 in row 3 (d = 4)
Penalty charges: ₹100 for 1st day late, ₹150 for 2nd, ₹200 for 3rd (d = ₹50)

concepts.name: nth Term of an AP — Finding Any Term Directly
concepts.real_life_application: Priya started a small business with ₹10,000 profit in Year 1. Profit increases by ₹2,000 each year. What will her profit be in Year 10? Using aₙ = a + (n-1)d with a = 10000, d = 2000, n = 10: a₁₀ = 10000 + 9(2000) = ₹28,000. She can plan her expansion without listing all 10 years!
concepts.purpose: The nth term formula aₙ = a + (n-1)d lets us jump to any term without listing the entire sequence. This is incredibly powerful for planning — you can predict the 50th or 100th term instantly.
day_to_day_usage: A taxi driver's daily earnings increase by ₹50 each day. His earnings on day 30 = first day + 29 × ₹50
A student's test scores improve by 3 marks each test. Score on 10th test = first score + 9 × 3
Annual rent increase: ₹12,000 in Year 1, ₹500 increase each year. Rent in Year 15 = 12000 + 14(500) = ₹19,000

concepts.name: Sum of n Terms of an AP — Cumulative Effect
concepts.real_life_application: Ravi saves ₹1000 in month 1, ₹1100 in month 2, ₹1200 in month 3 (increase of ₹100). How much will he save in total over 2 years (24 months)? Using Sₙ = n/2[2a + (n-1)d]: S₂₄ = 12[2000 + 23(100)] = 12[2000 + 2300] = 12 × 4300 = ₹51,600. That's his total savings for the down payment on a scooter!
concepts.purpose: The sum formula aggregates all terms in an AP. It's derived by adding the sequence forward and backward (the method Gauss discovered as a child). It's essential for financial planning, construction estimation, and many real-world cumulative calculations.
day_to_day_usage: Total money saved in a recurring deposit account over N months
Total number of seats in a theatre with 30 rows, each row having 2 more seats than the previous
Total distance traveled by a car accelerating uniformly (covered in Physics too!)
Total penalty paid for delayed bill payment over a week
Total earnings over a year with monthly salary increments

concepts.name: Arithmetic Mean — Finding the Middle Value
concepts.real_life_application: If the temperatures in Delhi on Monday and Wednesday are 30°C and 40°C, what should Tuesday's temperature be for a constant increase? The arithmetic mean A = (30+40)/2 = 35°C. The sequence 30, 35, 40 is an AP with d = 5. We 'inserted' one arithmetic mean (35) between 30 and 40.
concepts.purpose: The arithmetic mean of two numbers a and b is (a+b)/2. When we insert arithmetic means between two numbers, we're creating an AP. This concept is used in statistics, data interpolation, and creating evenly-spaced sequences.
day_to_day_usage: If a stock price was ₹100 on Monday and ₹180 on Wednesday, the Tuesday price for steady growth = (100+180)/2 = ₹140
Interpolating missing data between two known data points in a regular pattern
Creating equal installment amounts between two loan repayment dates

worked_examples.topic: Finding nth Term of an AP
worked_examples.problem: Find the 20th term of the AP: 5, 9, 13, 17, ...
board_mode: Given: First term a = 5, Common difference d = 9 - 5 = 4.
worked_examples.speed_mode: Golden step: Always find d first by subtracting any term from the next term. Then apply formula directly.
worked_examples.competitive_shortcut: 20th term = 5 + 19×4 = 5 + 76 = 81. For large n, compute (n-1)×d first, then add a.

worked_examples.problem: Find the sum of the first 15 terms of the AP: 7, 11, 15, 19, ...
board_mode: Alternative: First find last term l = a₁₅ = 7 + 14×4 = 63.
To Find: Sum of first 15 terms = 525.
worked_examples.speed_mode: Golden step: Use Sₙ = n/2(a + l) when the last term l is known or easy to find. It's simpler than the 2a + (n-1)d form.
worked_examples.competitive_shortcut: Check if there are pairing shortcuts: For 15 terms, (1st+last)×7.5 works — even easier mentally.

worked_examples.problem: Ravi's monthly savings follow an AP. He saves ₹800 in the first month, ₹950 in the second month, and ₹1100 in the third month. (a) How much will he save in the 12th month? (b) What will be his total savings after 2 years?
board_mode: Part (b): Total savings after 2 years = 24 months = S₂₄.
Ravi saves ₹2,450 in the 12th month and ₹60,600 in total over 2 years.
worked_examples.speed_mode: Golden step: Always extract a and d from the given sequence first. For total, use Sₙ formula. Check: does the answer make sense? ₹60,600 over 24 months ≈ ₹2,525/month average.
worked_examples.competitive_shortcut: For total after 2 years, note that average savings = (800 + 4250)/2 = ₹2,525. Total = 24 × 2525 = ₹60,600. Sum = n × average!

board_mode: Given: First term a = 2, Last term = 14. Total terms = 5 (2 numbers + 3 inserts).
Let the AP be: 2, a₂, a₃, a₄, 14.
worked_examples.speed_mode: Golden step: When inserting n means, total terms = n + 2. Use last term formula to find d, then generate means.
worked_examples.competitive_shortcut: The means are evenly spaced between 2 and 14. The gap between consecutive terms = (14-2)/(5-1) = 12/4 = 3. So terms: 2, 5, 8, 11, 14.

exercise_5_1.title: Exercise 5.1 — Identifying APs and Common Difference
exercise_5_1.objective: Identify arithmetic progressions and find the common difference

problems.question: Which of the following are APs? If they form an AP, find the common difference d and write the next three terms. (i) 2, 4, 8, 16, ... (ii) 2, 5/2, 3, 7/2, ... (iii) -1.2, -3.2, -5.2, -7.2, ... (iv) 3, 3 + √2, 3 + 2√2, 3 + 3√2, ...
solution: (i) 2, 4, 8, 16, ... Differences: 4-2=2, 8-4=4, 16-8=8. Differences are NOT constant → NOT an AP.
(ii) 2, 2.5, 3, 3.5, ... Differences: 2.5-2=0.5, 3-2.5=0.5, 3.5-3=0.5. Constant difference d=0.5 → IS an AP. Next three: 4, 4.5, 5.
problems.concept_insight: For an AP, the difference between consecutive terms must be constant. Check a₂-a₁ = a₃-a₂ = a₄-a₃ = ...

problems.question: Find the common difference of the AP: 3, 1, -1, -3, ... Is -150 a term of this AP?
solution: Step 3: Check if -150 is a term: 5 - 2n = -150 → -2n = -155 → n = 77.5.
Step 4: n = 77.5 is not an integer. Therefore, -150 is NOT a term of this AP.
problems.concept_insight: To check if a number is a term of an AP, set it equal to aₙ and solve for n. If n is a positive integer, it's a term.

problems.question: For what value of k will k, 2k+1, 5k-3 form an AP?
solution: Step 1: For three numbers to be in AP, 2(a₂) = a₁ + a₃ (property: twice the middle term = sum of extremes).
Verification: Terms are 2.5, 2(2.5)+1=6, 5(2.5)-3=9.5. AP with d = 3.5 ✓
problems.concept_insight: For three numbers a, b, c to be in AP: 2b = a + c. This is the 'Arithmetic Mean' property.

problems.question: Write the first four terms of the AP where a = -2 and d = 5.
problems.concept_insight: Each term is obtained by adding the common difference d to the previous term.

problems.question: Find the common difference and write the next term: √8, √18, √32, √50, ... (Hint: simplify the surds first)
problems.concept_insight: Always simplify surds first before checking for AP. Identical surd parts indicate a possible AP.

problems.question: The nth term of an AP is 7 - 4n. Find the common difference.
solution: Step 1: aₙ = 7 - 4n. To find the first term, put n=1: a₁ = 7-4=3.
Step 3: Common difference d = a₂ - a₁ = -1 - 3 = -4.
Alternative: In aₙ = An + B, d = A (coefficient of n). Here A = -4, so d = -4.
problems.concept_insight: If the nth term is given as a linear expression An + B, then d = A (the coefficient of n).

Step 4: The AP is: -2, 4, 10, 16, 22, ... (adding 6 each time).

problems.question: The sum of n terms of an AP is given by Sₙ = 2n² + 3n. Find the AP.
solution: Alternative: aₙ = Sₙ - Sₙ₋₁ = (2n²+3n) - [2(n-1)²+3(n-1)] = 4n+1. So a₁=5, a₂=9, etc.
problems.concept_insight: The nth term aₙ = Sₙ - Sₙ₋₁. This is a crucial relationship between sum and term.

Verification: Since d is not needed for n, we found it directly from a, l, and S.
problems.concept_insight: When a and l are known, use Sₙ = n/2(a+l). This is the simplest form — no need to find d.

exercise_5_4.title: Exercise 5.4 — AP Word Problems and Applications
exercise_5_4.objective: Solve real-life problems using AP concepts

problems.question: A manufacturer of TV sets produced 600 sets in the third year and 700 sets in the seventh year. Assuming production increases uniformly, find: (i) production in the 1st year (ii) production in the 10th year (iii) total production in 10 years.
solution: Step 1: Production in 3rd year = a₃ = a + 2d = 600.
Step 4: (i) Production in 1st year = a = 550 sets.
Step 5: (ii) Production in 10th year = a₁₀ = 550 + 9(25) = 550 + 225 = 775 sets.
Step 6: (iii) Total production in 10 years = S₁₀ = 10/2[2(550) + 9(25)] = 5[1100 + 225] = 5×1325 = 6625 sets.
problems.concept_insight: In production/savings problems with 'uniform increase', the quantities form an AP. Set up equations using given terms.

problems.question: A contractor agrees to build a road 5 km long in 100 days. He employs 50 labourers on day 1, 55 on day 2, 60 on day 3, and so on. Find his total labour-days of work.
solution: Step 1: Labourers per day form AP: 50, 55, 60, ... (a=50, d=5, n=100).
Step 2: Total labour-days = sum of labourers over 100 days.
problems.concept_insight: Labour-days = sum of workers per day. When workers increase uniformly, use AP sum formula.

topics.name: Selection of Terms in an AP
topics.concept: When solving problems with unknown terms of an AP, selecting terms appropriately can simplify calculations: (1) Three terms: a-d, a, a+d; (2) Four terms: a-3d, a-d, a+d, a+3d; (3) Five terms: a-2d, a-d, a, a+d, a+2d.
topics.formula: The sum of these symmetric selections often cancels the d terms, making equations simpler.

examples.problem: Find four numbers in AP whose sum is 20 and the sum of whose squares is 120.
solution: Step 1: Let the four numbers be a-3d, a-d, a+d, a+3d.
Step 6: Numbers for d=1: 2, 4, 6, 8. For d=-1: 8, 6, 4, 2.

topics.competitive_note: Symmetric term selection is a powerful JEE technique. For 3 terms, use (a-d, a, a+d). For 4 terms, use (a-3d, a-d, a+d, a+3d) to make sums cancel nicely.

topics.name: Problems on AP with Two Variables
topics.concept: When two APs are compared or combined, solve by setting up equations from the given conditions.
topics.formula: Use standard formulas aₙ = a+(n-1)d and Sₙ = n/2[2a+(n-1)d].

examples.problem: The ratio of the sum of n terms of two APs is (7n+1):(4n+27). Find the ratio of their nth terms.
solution: Step 1: Let the APs have first terms a₁, a₂ and common differences d₁, d₂.
Step 4: Replace n by (2n-1) in the sum ratio: (2a₁+(2n-2)d₁)/(2a₂+(2n-2)d₂) = (7(2n-1)+1)/(4(2n-1)+27).
Step 6: Therefore, ratio of nth terms = (14n-6)/(8n+23) = (7n-3)/(4n+11.5).

topics.competitive_note: This is a classic RD Sharma problem. The trick: replace n by (2n-1) in the sum ratio to get the nth term ratio.

past_papers.analysis_summary: Based on CBSE Class 10 board exams (2017-2026): Arithmetic Progressions consistently contributes 6-8 marks. nth term problems and sum of n terms are the most common questions (1-2 marks each). Word problems featuring real-life scenarios appear frequently in the long answer section.

short_answer_1_mark: Find the common difference given first two terms (asked in 2018, 2021, 2024)
State the formula for nth term or sum (asked in 2019, 2022, 2025)
short_answer_2_marks: Find the nth term given a and d (asked in 2020, 2022, 2024)
Find the number of terms in an AP (asked in 2017, 2021, 2023, 2026)
Check if a number is a term of a given AP (asked in 2019, 2023)
long_answer_4_marks: Word problem: production/savings forming AP (asked in 2018, 2021, 2024)
Find sum given two terms (asked in 2019, 2022, 2025)
Find AP given sum of n terms formula (asked in 2020, 2023, 2026)

scoring_areas: nth term formula — direct substitution, easy full marks
Sum formula — use Sₙ = n/2(a+l) when last term is known for simplicity
Word problems — identify a and d from description, set up equation, solve
Given two terms — form two equations, solve for a and d
common_mistakes: Using the wrong n in formulas: aₙ = a + (n-1)d, NOT a + nd
Sign errors with negative common difference
Forgetting to divide by 2 in sum formula: Sₙ = n/2[2a+(n-1)d], not n[2a+(n-1)d]
In word problems, not checking if n is a positive integer
Confusing aₙ (nth term) with Sₙ (sum of n terms)

complex.question: The ratio of the sum of n terms of two APs is (3n+5):(4n+3). Find the ratio of their 9th terms.

explanation.correct: Replace n by (2n-1): (3(2n-1)+5)/(4(2n-1)+3) = (6n-3+5)/(8n-4+3) = (6n+2)/(8n-1). For n=9: (54+2)/(72-1) = 56/71 = 32:39 (when simplified... 56:71, check: multiply by... hmm). (6(9)+2)/(8(9)-1) = (54+2)/(72-1) = 56/71. 56/71 ≠ 32/39. Let me recalculate: 3(17)+5 = 51+5=56, 4(17)+3 = 68+3=71. Ratio = 56:71. That doesn't match any option. Let me recompute: replace n by (2n-1). Ratio of nth terms = (3(2n-1)+5)/(4(2n-1)+3) = (6n-3+5)/(8n-4+3) = (6n+2)/(8n-1). For n=9: (54+2)/(72-1) = 56/71. None match. Actually the standard formula: if sum ratio = (an+b)/(cn+d), then nth term ratio = (a(2n-1)+b)/(c(2n-1)+d). Here (3(2n-1)+5)/(4(2n-1)+3). For n=9: (3×17+5)/(4×17+3) = (51+5)/(68+3) = 56/71. complex.question: The sum of three numbers in AP is 15. The sum of their squares is 83. Find the numbers.

explanation.correct: Let numbers be a-d, a, a+d. Sum=3a=15 → a=5. Sum of squares = (a-d)²+a²+(a+d)² = 3a²+2d² = 75+2d² = 83 → 2d²=8 → d²=4 → d=±2. Numbers: 3,5,7 or 7,5,3.

complex.question: If a, b, c are in AP, then which of the following is also in AP?

explanation.correct: If a,b,c are in AP: 2b = a+c. Check (c+a)-(b+c) = a-b; (a+b)-(c+a) = b-c. Since 2b=a+c, b-a = c-b, so a-b = -(b-a) = -(c-b) = b-c. So (b+c),(c+a),(a+b) are in AP with d = a-b = b-c.

wrong_options.1: a²,b²,c² in AP requires a²+c²=2b². For a=1,b=2,c=3: 1+9=10≠8. Not AP.
wrong_options.3: a-b, b-c, c-a: For 1,2,3: -1,-1,2. Not AP.

complex.question: If the sum of n terms of an AP is cn², find the common difference.

explanation.correct: Sₙ = cn². S₁ = c = a. S₂ = 4c = a+(a+d) = 2a+d = 2c+d → d=2c. Or: aₙ = Sₙ-Sₙ₋₁ = cn²-c(n-1)² = c(2n-1). Then d = a₂-a₁ = 3c-c = 2c.

wrong_options.1: d=c would give a₂-a₁=c, but actual difference between consecutive terms is 2c
wrong_options.2: c/2 is half the correct answer

complex.question: If the pth term of an AP is q and the qth term is p, prove that its (p+q)th term is 0.

explanation.correct: aₚ = a+(p-1)d = q, a_q = a+(q-1)d = p. Subtract: (p-q)d = q-p → (p-q)d = -(p-q) → d = -1 (if p≠q). Then a+(p-1)(-1) = q → a-p+1 = q → a = p+q-1. Now aₚ₊_q = a+(p+q-1)d = (p+q-1)+(p+q-1)(-1) = 0. Proved ✓.

wrong_options.1: The statement is mathematically proven TRUE above
wrong_options.2: The proof works for all p≠q; if p=q, they're the same term
wrong_options.3: It can be determined and is always true

vedic_math_shortcuts.title: Ādyam-Ādyena (आद्यमाद्येन) — 'First by First' / Sum of Series
vedic_math_shortcuts.concept: The sum of an AP can be found by multiplying the average of first and last terms by the number of terms. For consecutive natural numbers (1+2+...+n), the sum is n(n+1)/2 — known as the 'Gauss formula' but also found in Vedic texts.
vedic_math_shortcuts.real_numbers_application: Quick computation of totals: total savings, total seats, total production — any situation where quantities increase uniformly.

common_misconceptions: The common difference can only be positive — FALSE: d can be negative (decreasing AP) or zero (constant AP).
The nth term formula is aₙ = a + nd — FALSE: It is aₙ = a + (n-1)d. The first term has n=1, so no d is added.
An AP must always increase or decrease — FALSE: A constant sequence (d=0) like 5,5,5,5,... is also an AP.
Sum of n terms formula always gives an integer — FALSE: The sum can be a fraction if terms are fractions.
If a, b, c are in AP, then a², b², c² are also in AP — FALSE: Example: 1,2,3 are in AP but 1,4,9 are not.
You cannot find the sum of an AP without knowing the common difference — FALSE: If a and l (last term) are known, Sₙ = n/2(a+l) doesn't need d.
All sequences with a pattern are APs — FALSE: Only sequences with constant difference are APs. Geometric (multiplying) sequences are not APs.
The sum of n terms of an AP is always n times the middle term — TRUE (for odd n): The middle term equals the average of first and last terms.
